title: Logger class diagram
idea: The logger's class design splits one job into five types: a Logger filters, a LogRecord carries facts, a LogLevel ranks, an Appender writes, a Formatter shapes text.

analogy.text: A mail room. The clerk (Logger) rejects junk mail, and each courier (Appender) packs letters in its own envelope style (Formatter).
analogy.breaks: One letter goes to one place; a record goes to every appender.

points: `Logger` owns a name, a threshold and a list of appenders.
`LogRecord` is an immutable value: level, logger name, message, time, thread.
`Appender` and `Formatter` are interfaces, so outputs and layouts swap freely.
Each appender holds its own formatter: console can be plain while files are JSON.

edges.label: uses
edges.caption: A Logger compares each call's LogLevel against its own threshold.

edges.label: creates
edges.caption: Only accepted calls become a LogRecord, built once per call.

edges.label: has 0..*
edges.caption: The Logger hands that one record to each of its appenders.

edges.label: has-a
edges.caption: Each Appender asks its own Formatter to turn the record into text.

edges.label: is-a
edges.caption: ConsoleAppender implements Appender and writes to a PrintStream.

edges.label: is-a
edges.caption: FileAppender implements Appender and writes to a file. New outputs are new classes.

code.title: The model in Java
code.caption: The five types with their invariants. A list stands in for the console so the output is easy to read.

walk.text: A plain formatter, one appender, and an `orders` logger at INFO.
DEBUG is dropped by the threshold; ERROR reaches the appender.
Building a record without a level breaks an invariant and is refused.
An immutable record; the compact constructor requires level and name, and turns a null message into empty text.
Two single-method interfaces: the swap points of the whole design.
Logger copies its appender list, so callers cannot change it later.
`log` filters first, then builds one record and fans it out.

pitfalls: Do not put formatting inside `Logger`; each output may need a different layout.
Do not make `LogRecord` mutable; appenders may read it on other threads.
Avoid a class per level (`ErrorLogger`); a level is data, not a type.

quiz.q: What is the last line LoggerModel prints?
quiz.why: The compact constructor calls `requireNonNull` with a message. The exception carries that message, and the catch prints it.

takeaway: Logger filters, LogRecord carries, Appender writes, Formatter shapes, LogLevel ranks.

starters: Why does each Appender own a Formatter instead of the Logger?
Should LogRecord also carry key-value context like a request id?
Is Logger a good candidate for the singleton pattern?
